lines.text: A home's features determine its comfort, character, and market value. In British homes, the kitchen is often described as the heart of the house — modern open-plan kitchen-diners have replaced the separate galley kitchens of older properties. Fitted kitchens with integrated appliances (dishwasher, oven, hob, and extractor hood) are standard in newer homes. Central heating — typically a gas boiler system with radiators — keeps homes warm through the long British winters. Double glazing (two panes of glass with an insulating gap) is now expected; older single-glazed windows are draughty and energy-inefficient. Period homes may feature original fireplaces, ceiling roses, cornicing, and sash windows — architectural details that add significant value. Loft conversions add extra bedrooms or offices without extending the footprint, while conservatories — glass-walled garden rooms — extend living space with natural light. Gardens are prized: a south-facing garden (catching maximum sunlight) commands a premium. Inside, fitted wardrobes maximise bedroom storage, while underfloor heating is an increasingly popular alternative to radiators. Smart home features — programmable thermostats, smart lighting, and video doorbells — are becoming standard in new-builds. Energy efficiency is now a key selling point: solar panels, cavity wall insulation, and high EPC ratings attract environmentally conscious buyers and reduce running costs.
